blocks.title: Linked list
blocks.md: A **linked list** is a chain of **nodes**; each node holds data and a **pointer** (the index or address of the next node). The **head** pointer marks the start; the last node's pointer is null. Inserting or deleting in the middle only changes pointers (no shifting of items), but finding the k-th item requires following k pointers. Pseudocode here is Python-like (indentation = block).

blocks.title: Binary search tree (BST)
blocks.md: A **tree** has a **root** and nodes with **children**; a **leaf** has none. In a **binary** tree each node has at most two children. In a **BST**, for every node all keys in the left subtree are smaller and all keys in the right subtree are larger. To insert: compare with the root and go left or right until an empty place is found.

blocks.caption: A binary search tree with root 50, children 30 and 70, and leaves 20, 40, 60 and 80.
blocks.alt: BST diagram: root 50; left child 30 with leaves 20 and 40; right child 70 with leaves 60 and 80.

blocks.title: Traversals
blocks.md: **In-order** (left, root, right) gives a BST's keys in ascending order. **Pre-order** (root, left, right) is used to copy a tree. **Post-order** (left, right, root) is used to delete a tree or evaluate an expression tree. The **height** is the number of levels.

blocks.title: Hash tables
blocks.md: A **hash table** stores items at an index computed by a **hash function** from the key (e.g. key MOD table size). Lookup is very fast on average. A **collision** is when two keys give the same index; it is handled, for example, by **chaining** (a list at each slot) or by probing the next free slot.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Searching a BST that was built from sorted data is slow because it becomes a chain.
- Inserting a node: update **both** pointers (new node's next and previous node's next).
- In-order traversal sorts only a **binary search** tree.
- A good hash function spreads keys evenly.

blocks.title: Example 1 - Traversals
blocks.statement: For the tree built by inserting 50, 30, 70, 20, 40, 60, 80, list the in-order and pre-order traversals.

blocks.title: Example 2 - Hash
blocks.statement: Use hash = key MOD 7 to place keys 15, 22, 9 in a table of 7 slots (0-6). Show collisions.
steps: 15 and 22 collide at slot 1: with chaining slot 1 holds the list 15, 22.

blocks.title: Recursion
blocks.md: A **recursive** subroutine calls itself on a **smaller** version of the problem. It needs a **base case** (stops the recursion) and a **recursive case**. Pseudocode here is Python-like (indentation = block). def fact(n): if n == 0: return 1 else: return n \* fact(n - 1). Each call is stored as a **stack frame**; too many nested calls cause a **stack overflow**.

blocks.title: Tracing
blocks.md: Trace by writing each call until the base case, then **unwind**: fact(3) = 3 x fact(2) = 3 x 2 x fact(1) = 3 x 2 x 1 x fact(0) = 3 x 2 x 1 x 1 = 6. Recursion suits problems with self-similar structure: trees, divide-and-conquer, Towers of Hanoi. A loop is often faster and uses less memory.

blocks.caption: Table comparing about how many steps grow for n equal to 1024.
blocks.alt: Table of growth: log n 10, n 1024, n log n 10240 and n squared 1048576.

blocks.title: Big-O notation
blocks.md: **Big-O** describes how running time (or memory) grows with input size n in the worst case, ignoring constants. **O(1)** constant; **O(log n)** logarithmic (binary search); **O(n)** linear (linear search); **O(n log n)** (merge sort); **O(n²)** quadratic (bubble sort, nested loops); **O(2ⁿ)** exponential (naive Fibonacci).

blocks.title: Merge sort (outline)
blocks.md: Divide the list into halves until each has one item, then **merge** sorted halves repeatedly. It always takes about n log n steps but needs extra memory. **Quick sort** picks a pivot and partitions the list; it is O(n log n) on average but O(n²) in the worst case.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Forgetting the base case gives infinite recursion.
- The recursive call must move **towards** the base case.
- Big-O ignores constants: 5n and n are both O(n).
- O(n²) is not 'twice as slow': doubling n quadruples the time.

blocks.title: Example 1 - Trace
blocks.statement: def fact(n): if n == 0: return 1 else: return n \* fact(n - 1). Trace fact(4).
steps: fact(4) = 4 x fact(3) = 4 x 3 x fact(2) = 4 x 3 x 2 x fact(1) = 4 x 3 x 2 x 1 x fact(0).
fact(0) = 1, so the result is 4 x 3 x 2 x 1 x 1 = 24.

blocks.title: Example 2 - Towers of Hanoi
blocks.statement: The minimum number of moves for n discs satisfies moves(n) = 2 x moves(n-1) + 1, moves(0) = 0. Find moves(5).
